sources.quote: Among internists who received no payments, for example, the average brand-name prescribing rate was about 20 percent, compared to about 30 percent for those who received more than $5,000.
sources.searcher_note: Same finding, same direction (brand-name share rises with payments, highest above $5,000) in five specialties, but 2014 data, not 2024; no cost-per-claim multiple. NPR ran the same story the same day (copy, not recorded).

sources.quote: Across the 12 specialties examined, a dose-response relationship was observed in which greater payments were associated with greater prescribing costs per patient.
sources.searcher_note: 2013 Open Payments + Part D: cost per patient rises with payments in every one of 12 specialties; also 'Similar associations were observed with proportion of branded prescriptions written.' Cost per patient, not per claim.

sources.quote: A physician-industry financial relationship was associated with increased odds of prescribing costly brand-name drugs of uncertain medical benefit.
sources.searcher_note: 2014 data, six specific costly brand drugs; same direction.

sources.quote: Furthermore, studies have shown that HCPs who receive remuneration from a company are more likely to prescribe or order that company
sources.searcher_note: Special Fraud Alert on speaker programs; general statement of the pattern, no numbers.

sources.outlet: National Bureau of Economic Research (Carey, Lieber, Miller)
sources.quote: Physicians receiving payments from the firms experiencing the patent expiry transition their patients just as quickly to generics as physicians who do not receive such payments.
sources.searcher_note: Partial disagreement: on 2013-15 data, paid doctors switch to generics at patent expiry as fast as unpaid ones, and drug quality largely unaffected; but same paper finds prescribing of paid-for drugs rises after payment. Working paper Feb 2020, revised Mar 2021 (day not given).

notes: Well-worn pattern since ProPublica 2016 (brand share vs payments) and PLOS One 2016 (cost per patient vs payments, all 12 specialties). No source found using 2024 data, a $10K+ threshold, 7 specialties, or a cost-per-claim multiple (1.2-5.6x; internal medicine $94 to $355). Recent 2026 items found were payment-total roundups (Medscape 2026, 402 paywall; AHIP analysis of 2024 brand-maker payments, 403) and were not recorded. Annals of Internal Medicine 2021 systematic review (30 of 36 studies positive) returned 403/captcha on both publisher and PubMed; not recorded.
